symptom: a headache and a runny nose that would not dry up
hook: air had crept in and sat over the front of the brain like a bubble under a phone screen protector
whatYouSee: Dark pockets of air sit inside the skull at the front pressing on the brain behind the forehead.
whyItMatters: Pneumocephaly is air inside the skull and is a complication of a fracture of the skull base. A fracture of the anterior skull base can also give the raccoon eye sign.
treatment: Treatment may include observation with head elevation since small amounts of air often absorb. A persistent leak or air under tension may need surgical repair of the torn dura.
takeaway: Air inside the skull after a head injury means the skull base has been breached until proven otherwise.

condition.keyFindings: Lateral skull radiograph. Irregular lobulated very dark (radiolucent) air collections lie inside the skull just beneath the inner table of the frontal bone and outline the anterior surface of the frontal lobes, forming a dark crescent behind the forehead and over the anterior cranial fossa. Because this is a lateral view both frontal regions are superimposed. A faint fracture line crosses the floor of the anterior cranial fossa. The rest of the skull vault, the sella turcica, the facial bones, the mandible and the upper cervical spine look normal and the brain elsewhere is uniform grey.

defects: Unexplained additional image findings: ["Multiple well-defined rounded radiolucent lesions clustered in the frontal and anterior parietal calvarium — these represent lytic calvarial lesions (myeloma/metastases pattern), not intracranial air collections consistent with traumatic pneumocephalus"]

findings: Lateral projection skull and upper cervical spine radiograph

Multiple well-defined rounded radiolucent lesions clustered predominantly in the frontal and anterior parietal calvarium, varying in size from approximately 5–20 mm, with relatively well-defined margins and no visible sclerotic rim on most lesions
The lesions are concentrated in the frontal bone and extend toward the vertex anteriorly
Calvarium cortical outline otherwise appears intact at the posterior and superior vault
Sella turcica appears within normal limits on this projection
Upper cervical spine visible with no gross bony destruction identified
Dentition present with tooth roots visible; mandible appears intact
No evidence of midline shift assessable on plain radiograph
differential: Multiple myeloma (plasmacytoma of the skull — classical 'punched-out' lytic lesions without sclerotic rim)
Metastatic disease to the calvarium (lytic metastases, e.g., from breast, lung, renal, or thyroid primary)
Langerhans cell histiocytosis (eosinophilic granuloma — lytic calvarial lesions, which can be geographic or beveled-edge; clustered frontal predominance is compatible)
anatomyConcerns: The lesions are clustered asymmetrically in the anterior calvarium which is anatomically plausible for pathology but unusual for a single incidental finding; artifact or overlying foreign material is considered unlikely given consistent rounded morphology and varying sizes
Projection is a true lateral; slight rotation cannot be fully excluded but facial bones appear reasonably superimposed
No acquisition artifacts such as motion blur or positioning collimation errors that would obscure diagnosis are noted
